newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech parliament approves 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Czech parliament approves 1997 budget.

text.p: The lower house of the Czech parliament on Friday approved the draft 1997 state budget, a major victory for the minority administration of conservative Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus.

The centre-right coalition's fifth straight balanced budget was approved with equal revenue and expenditure of 549.1 billion crowns ($20 billion), up from the revised 1996 budget of 491 billion ($18 billion).
The plan was approved with the minimum required 99 deputies in the 200-seat chamber voting in favour, including two opposition Social Democrats, with 96 against and five not voting.

Of 23 line-item amendments put to a vote before the final package was approved, only three spending increases above the government draft were accepted, totalling 122.55 million crowns ($4.51 million), including an extra 100 million ($3.68 million) for the agriculture budget.

It kept the corporate income tax rate at 39 percent, ending a junior coalition party's move to lower it to 35 percent, and extended the required period for holding securities before getting a waiver on capital gains tax to six months from three.

The three-party coalition led by Klaus's Civic Democratic Party (ODS) fell two seats short of a majority in the 200-seat Chamber in June elections, and the budget vote was seen as crucial to the survival of the minority government.
But in October four members of the opposition Social Democrats broke party ranks to allow the draft 1997 budget to get through the parliament's first reading.

"I believe that while considering the draft, the rational opinion will prevail. I believe that the budget will pass and the Czech Republic will have another balanced budget," Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik told the chamber before the final vote.

One dissident opposition deputy, budget committee chairman Jozef Wagner, summed up less his than enthusiastic support for the government budget when he told the chamber: "Our goal is to approve a budget simply to allow the functioning of the state."

President Havel, recuperating from cancer surgery on his lungs, sent a message from the hospital asking deputies to "decide not only according to your party's disposition, but also with a view toward the stability, prosperity and trust in our country".

On Thursday, coalition leaders said they had reached a compromise after a junior partner, the Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA), demanded a commitment to a deregulation plan on energy and housing rents and tax cuts.
The three party leaders agreed to appease ODA by completing the deregulations and tax cut schedule by the year 2000, the end of the government's current term.

The 1997 budget is based on expected growth in gross domestic product of 5.4 percent average annual inflation of 8.6 percent, a current account deficit of 5.8 percent and average unemployment of 3.3 percent:
Full-year 1996 GDP growth is forecast at around 4.8 percent with inflation of around nine percent, a current deficit of seven percent, and unemployment of just over three percent.

The government said on Wednesday, however, that the 1996 budget, which was approved as a balanced budget, may end with a deficit totalling 1.2 billion Czech crowns ($44 million), because of lower than expected revenues from taxes and foreign debt repayment.
